metadata.title: OpenClaw Evolutionary Coding Lab: connecting the pieces
metadata.description: Reproducible source, cancellation experiments, and the path to one complete, controlled coding task.

outcome.summary: A file-only library layout passes the supervised evaluator run, and actual files now form an ordered launcher deployment proposal. Full runtime acceptance, original native startup and a real coding task remain unfinished.

provenance.summary: AI-assisted project update checked against local source and recorded development validation through September 26, 2026. Engine evidence remains local. Public references document the article and publication process; they do not independently reproduce engine results.

sections.title: Where the Lab stands

blocks.text: OpenClaw Evolutionary Coding Lab is an experimental, locally operated system for carrying out bounded coding tasks. The intended workflow starts with a task and explicit limits, makes changes in an isolated copy of a project, evaluates the result and returns a patch for human review.

The Lab already has project tracking, planning, task scheduling, reporting and mechanisms that control which actions a task may perform. Development fixtures also exercise parts of the execution system. The current challenge is connecting those components into one demonstrable workflow, including what happens when work fails or is stopped.

blocks.label: Current status
blocks.text: The revised filter, native build and protected evaluator sources agree. The evaluator also runs with the proposed file-only library layout. Actual files now form an ordered launcher deployment proposal, with checked identities and byte preimages. The remaining deployment roles, installed custody, platform acceptance, original native startup and a real coding task are still unfinished. No engine release has been published.

blocks.alt: Intended workflow, with integration still in progress: scope and authorize a task with exact source and limits; claim the attempt once and reject replay; run and evaluate changes in an isolated copy; return the patch and test results for human review while preserving the original project.
blocks.caption: Figure 1. The intended workflow. A complete end-to-end demonstration is still pending.

sections.title: What has been verified

items.label: Source-v10 offline validation
items.value: The extracted snapshot ran 1,612 tests with no unexpected failures, errors or skips. That total includes one expected historical failure; 17 named machine-specific checks were excluded.

items.label: Repeatable source export
items.value: All 615 selected source files retained their recorded hashes after testing. Re-exporting the extracted files with the archived executable permissions restored produced a byte-for-byte identical archive.

items.label: Execution fixtures
items.value: Disposable test programs exercised launch settings, sealed executable data, output limits, deadlines, cleanup within a process group and Windows-to-Linux handoff.

items.label: Release materials
items.value: Two isolated builds produced identical Python packages. A fresh Linux installation used that package without downloading dependencies; all 74 installed module files matched, and the synthetic offline demo passed. MIT licensing, third-party notices and release documentation are prepared.

blocks.text: These results apply to specific development artifacts. The offline suite did not rerun the earlier native execution experiments, and the package's demo exercises a synthetic project registry without running coding tasks. The engine source has not yet been published as a GitHub release; the linked portfolio repository hosts this article.

sections.title: Integration progress: stopping work reliably

blocks.text: Three executor gaps were reproduced with disposable test processes and corrected. A child closing both output streams no longer disables its deadline. Interrupting capture now stops and reaps the direct child before the original interruption returns to the caller. A pipe held open outside the stopped process group can no longer keep cleanup waiting indefinitely: an incomplete read is reported as an execution error.

That executor snapshot passed a full offline run of 1,591 tests with no unexpected failures, errors or skips. One historical expected failure and 17 explicitly excluded machine-specific checks remain. The tested source hashes were checked at the time of validation. Focused validation also passed 79 checks covering the new regressions and existing execution and one-shot authority behavior.

A separate Windows-to-Linux development fixture also passed two cases after a child and grandchild confirmed they were running: an explicit cancel message, and closure of the input connection. Linux reported the direct child reaped by the executor, the grandchild reaped after termination, and no remaining children. The host observed completion in 247 ms and 211 ms. This is cooperative cancellation evidence for that disposable workload, not proof for forcibly killing the Windows launcher or for descendants that escape containment.

blocks.label: Scope of this result
blocks.text: These corrections were subsequently included in the verified source-v10 snapshot. Complete cross-host cancellation, escaped-descendant containment, production qualification and a real coding task remain unfinished.

sections.title: Keeping a result when the requester disappears

blocks.text: Forcibly terminating the Windows requester exposed a gap: the known Linux processes disappeared, but no completion report survived. That experiment remains inconclusive. A separate backend was then tested so the work and its reporting could outlive the requester's connection.

In the latest disposable experiment, Windows terminated the requester after the worker confirmed readiness. The backend detected the disconnect, requested cancellation, confirmed direct-child and grandchild cleanup, and saved a terminal execution-failure result. A separate process reopened the store and read that result. Windows termination took 282 ms; the worker reported completion in 113 ms. These are observations from one experiment, not performance guarantees.

The executor now accepts an explicit cancellation signal and returns a failure observation that the existing task pipeline can save. Focused validation passed 82 execution and authority checks plus a pipeline test showing a persisted failure and no replay launch. A broader pipeline run passed 179 of 182 tests; the other three failed because installed Python or standard-library bytes did not match pinned runtime requirements. Those exact checks were already excluded from the offline profile. Their failures remain unresolved runtime qualification work.

blocks.label: What this establishes
blocks.text: The backend experiment and pipeline regression exercise separate boundaries. They do not yet prove a complete authenticated coding service, service restart recovery, concurrent request handling or containment of escaped descendants. These changes were subsequently included in source-v10; newer worker safeguards remain outside that snapshot.

sections.title: Recovering dispatch and completion records

blocks.text: The explicit-cancellation snapshot subsequently passed a full offline run of 1,595 tests with no unexpected failures, errors or skips. One historical expected failure and 17 named host-dependent exclusions remain. The recorded input hashes still matched after the run. This result predates the recovery adapters described below.

New review-stage code reuses the existing database transaction to save the exact dispatch record when a task is consumed. It can recover that record after a lost response without consuming the task again. A second adapter saves the bound execution evidence and its evaluated outcome together, then re-evaluates that evidence when the store is reopened. It accepts no caller-selected verdict.

Seventeen targeted checks passed across the recovery and cancellation work. Separate-process tests showed that conflicting valid outcomes have one winner, identical submissions create only one terminal transition, and a result survives an abrupt process exit immediately after commit. Other checks reject incomplete or forged evidence and preserve failed-test and execution-failure outcomes.

blocks.label: Component recovery, not service qualification
blocks.text: These recovery adapters are included in source-v10, but still use synthetic witness evidence and are not connected to production task dispatch. The transport contract requires a root-owned systemd socket and authenticated deployment identities. Accepted runtime and policy setup, live worker authentication and complete workflow recovery remain unfinished.

sections.title: Worker safeguards added after source-v10

blocks.text: The receiving path now checks the real Linux identity of both the process that connected and the process sending each message. It also verifies message framing, ordering and exact task bytes, and rejects unexpected attached file descriptors. Twenty-one transport and binding checks passed, including two real child-process tests showing that an inherited socket cannot hide a different sender. Binding tests still use synthetic deployment records.

Durable claims now record the suite and each individual step before any future launcher handoff. A step requires valid evidence matching the saved claims for earlier steps. Missing, altered, out-of-order or terminal-failure evidence cannot unlock another step, and reopening an existing claim does not create a new one. Fifteen suite and step-claim tests passed, including concurrent suite claims, partial writes and replay after reopening.

blocks.label: What remains unproven
blocks.text: These component checks preceded the combined checkout validation below. They do not qualify a protected running service. Source-v10 remains the last verified packaged snapshot and does not include the newer handshake and delivery work.

sections.title: Connecting saved tasks to the worker

blocks.text: A compatibility review found that the first Python handshake used the predecessor V1 format while the existing native successor requires V2. The new codec follows the successor's closed records and length-prefixed packets, and rejects V1 fallback. Separate Python processes now complete that V2 exchange, derive the same connection identity and transfer the exact task bytes. This has not yet been tested against a running native launcher.

The exchange retains socket and process handles. Checks reject a valid queued response from a worker that has already exited, altered task bytes, transfer before authentication and a second request on the same session. Larger binary requests are split into checked messages; the receiver returns no partial task.

A review adapter now recovers the exact saved dispatch, sends it through the V2 session and saves the worker's suite claim only after the complete task is verified. Redelivery through a new connection recovers the existing claim rather than creating a fresh one. The successful integration fixture explicitly simulates protected-role admission; its database, Linux credentials, process handles, message transfer and claim storage are real. Without that simulation, the fixture process is correctly rejected as a protected principal.

The combined development checkout ran 1,692 offline tests with no unexpected failures, errors or skips. One historical expected failure and 17 named host-dependent exclusions remain. All 643 recorded source inputs retained their hashes, lengths and archive permission classification after the run. This validates the checkout; it is not a new package, native qualification result or completed coding demonstration.

blocks.label: The next integration boundary
blocks.text: The saved review dispatch still derives from predecessor authority bindings. V2 transport does not migrate or accept the full runtime-policy model. The remaining work must join successor policy, independently accepted deployment and runtime custody, per-step execution claims and the native launcher before demonstrating a complete coding task.

sections.title: Checking the runtime pieces together

blocks.text: A new review path checks the proposed source set, worker identities, deployment contents, launcher journal and six communication endpoints together. It verifies actual supplied program and configuration bytes, rederives their identities and checks that journal references point to the reviewed launcher. This prevents a caller from substituting unchecked deployment records between those component checks.

Thirty-three focused checks passed across this work and source packaging validation. They reject changed executable bytes, missing inputs, swapped worker roles, older configurations presented as the successor, altered journal policies and weakened endpoint permissions. These tests use synthetic deployment fixtures; they do not establish that the protected services are installed or running correctly.

The service review also exposed a remaining gap: the successor schema permits a nonempty service-policy object, while the native service-record check does not fully validate that object's contents. The older Python validator enforces an older service contract and cannot simply be reused unchanged. The next step is an exact successor service policy tied to its operational requirements, followed by checks of the actual service and its protected directories.

blocks.label: Development checks, not runtime acceptance
blocks.text: These additions postdate the full 1,692-test run and are covered by the 33 focused checks only. Source-v10 remains the last verified packaged snapshot. The combined review grants no execution permission; full runtime acceptance, native integration and the complete coding demonstration remain open.

sections.title: Testing the native startup path

blocks.text: An exact successor service-policy proposal now preserves the existing lifecycle protections and includes the successor's containment and journal requirements. The focused source, runtime and packaging checks reached 40 passing tests. This remains a proposed policy encoding; it has not been accepted as a running service configuration.

Disposable startup probes exposed practical deployment requirements. The first stopped because the service account did not exist. After a dedicated non-login launcher account was provisioned, the next probe showed that its temporary filesystem suppressed file capabilities and that systemd supplied a supplementary group. A third probe on a capability-enabled filesystem demonstrated the required capability state and successfully cleared that group. Temporary privileged files and probe services were removed; the dedicated account remains.

A separate launcher patch clears only the expected redundant primary-group entry at startup and keeps the later credential checks strict. Eight isolated behavior cases passed, including foreign groups and syscall failures. The first binary build used an older link recipe and failed the symbol-visibility check; a separate build with the reviewed linker policy passed the static checks. Both outcomes are retained.

Listener inspection then found a native defect: the code compared a filesystem socket inode with the different inode belonging to its open socket descriptor, rejecting a valid listener. The proposed repair asks the kernel to bind the exact socket identity to its filesystem entry. Its build and static checks passed, and the response parser rejected malformed and truncated inputs. An initial parser test harness crashed because of its entry-point stack alignment; the corrected harness passed.

The exact native helper then passed four real-kernel fixture cases: accepting a valid listener, rejecting the old listener after its pathname was replaced, accepting the replacement listener, and rejecting an unbound socket. All temporary sockets were removed. This tests the repair independently of the complete launcher.

blocks.label: Still before a complete coding run
blocks.text: The repaired full launcher has been built and inspected, but has not been executed. These results do not establish accepted source/build contracts, protected service custody, complete runtime acceptance or a coding-task outcome. The next work connects those requirements before demonstrating success, failure, restart and cancellation. The earlier full-suite and packaged-snapshot results remain separate.

sections.title: Preserving history across startup and recovery

blocks.text: Concrete service and socket configurations now pass the service manager's offline verifier. They describe the launch identity, restricted capabilities, communication endpoints, cleanup behavior and journal directories. Verification used synthetic role records and an inert executable placeholder; these configurations have not been installed or used to start the complete launcher.

Journal review found another startup gap: when its main state file was missing, the code created fresh counters without first checking for saved history. A separate repair permits initialization only when the protected journal has exactly its expected empty structure. Existing records, receipts, partial state files or unexpected entries cause startup to stop. Eleven tests of the exact native directory helper passed without changing fixture contents or retained directory positions.

A second fixture exercised the actual journal's initialization, locking, reservation and recovery code inside an isolated filesystem. It passed eleven cases using real saved files and operating-system locks. Restart preserved the state bytes, the wrong writer and a competing lock holder were rejected, and missing or corrupt control state left the remaining history unchanged.

To test interrupted work, the fixture saved a reservation and exited before publishing its result. On reopening, recovery permanently marked that reservation unusable, preserved the journal's identity and kept its sequence numbers moving forward. Repeating recovery changed nothing. This prevents that reserved range from being reused; it does not claim the interrupted coding task completed.

The first integration runner stopped at sandbox argument validation before the native fixture executed. A corrected runner passed, and all disposable state was removed. The combined launcher proposal also passed its five-stage build and static image checks. The earlier full-suite count and source-v10 package remain separate from these newer changes.

blocks.label: What this proves—and what remains
blocks.text: This is journal-component evidence using synthetic deployment identities. Interruption was a deliberate exit after reservation, not a test of every possible crash point. Complete launcher execution, recovery of committed transactions, final service custody and acceptance of the changed source and runtime still need verification before the full coding demonstration.

sections.title: Joining build contracts to real service behavior

blocks.text: The combined startup-repair candidate was built independently twice, producing identical intermediate outputs and executables. Review then found that two new helper includes did not fit the deployment contract's closed source-file set. Incorporating their exact code into the owning files restored that structure without changing either object file or the executable; only an assembly source-line comment changed.

A proposed contract for that source layout passes the existing Python cross-source checks. The exact native contract validator also passed fifteen fixture cases: accepting matching source records and rejecting altered digests, missing or duplicate roles, incorrect lengths or types, and weakened contract rules with recalculated identities. These records use synthetic deployment data and do not establish trusted runtime acceptance.

A native service-policy test reproduced a separate gap: the earlier validator accepted an empty policy when the surrounding record identity matched. The proposed fix checks the complete reviewed policy. Thirty-two cases passed, including mutations of every one of its twenty-nine fields with freshly calculated record identities. The updated complete launcher builds and passes static inspection; the earlier reproducibility result does not cover this later binary.

An inert temporary service then exercised selected proposed settings on the actual service manager. All twenty-five checks passed, covering identity settings, controller delegation and ownership, stopping and restart settings, a private mount namespace, and the shared host PID namespace. The inert process had no file capabilities, so this does not qualify the native launcher's complete credential state.

A further fixture tested real systemd socket activation through the exact native descriptor-admission functions. The first attempt stopped before the fixture ran because its synthetic sender groups did not exist. A separate attempt provisioned temporary empty groups and passed: the native code admitted three null standard streams and exactly two listeners, checked their kernel-to-filesystem identities and ownership, and joined their groups to the fixture's expected roles. All test units, sockets, files and temporary groups were removed.

blocks.label: The remaining combined test
blocks.text: These are verified component boundaries. They have not yet run together as the full privileged launcher with accepted source/build inputs, trusted deployment records, credential bootstrap, journal custody and protected task execution. That complete startup and coding demonstration remains the next major milestone. The historical 1,692-test run and source-v10 package do not include these later repairs.

sections.title: Closing the evaluator configuration gap

blocks.text: The native credential bootstrap and socket handoff have now passed together in one disposable service fixture. It used the launcher's original startup and credential-checking code, then admitted the two real systemd listeners and checked credentials again. The expected user and group, empty supplementary groups and exact capability set held before and after admission. This still replaces the launcher's main workflow with a test body; it does not execute the complete startup path.

The first combined runner stopped while creating its temporary groups, before the privileged executable or service ran. A separate runner with shorter group names passed. Temporary privileged files, service units, sockets and groups were removed afterward. The dedicated launcher account from the earlier setup remains.

Thirteen exact runtime and review inputs have been staged as non-executable candidate data. Tracing the remaining startup requirements exposed a configuration mismatch: the native launcher reads the successor profile, while the existing Python evaluator opens the predecessor profile path and rejects the valid successor profile even when its source digest is correct. The evaluator also still calls the predecessor runtime-lock parser. Packaging that evaluator unchanged would not produce a working successor runtime.

A separate successor evaluator component now checks all twelve platform observations against the reviewed source set. It derives classifications from raw evidence and rejects incomplete, reordered or malformed observations, wrong error-number pairs, altered source bytes and substitution of the predecessor profile. The probe definitions and interpretation rules are unchanged between the two profiles; the old evaluator parser remains intact.

Service-policy review is also connected to freshly checked runtime components. The service must refer to the launcher and reaper deployments validated in that same review, with matching source and configuration bytes and the expected activation identity. The combined runtime, evaluator and source suite passes forty-nine focused tests. These use synthetic offline evidence and do not grant execution permission or replace the earlier full-suite result.

blocks.label: Immediate next step
blocks.text: Complete successor runtime-lock and nested acceptance checks, including deployment, filesystem and process-custody joins. Then connect the evaluator's fixed entry point and measured Python dependencies, exercise full startup, and run the controlled coding demonstration. No complete launcher startup or real coding task has run yet.

sections.title: Connecting successor validation from configuration to measurements

blocks.text: The successor evaluator now checks a complete runtime configuration against its source files and supplied program bytes. It joins the five deployment roles, service settings, communication endpoints, stores and journals, and checks that declared filter and configuration hashes match their exact deployment roles. The complete fixture uses the required reaper filter bytes, rather than the small synthetic filter used in earlier geometry tests.

Nested platform and mount-isolation results are rederived from their observations. Recalculating a record identity cannot preserve a forged passing flag, substitute another verifier, or combine results from different platform measurements. The earlier accepted measurement bundle must also match the reviewed configuration and its complete platform record.

Challenge integration exposed another predecessor assumption: the old check expected a store-reference field that the new file-based launcher journal does not have. A separate successor check follows the native launcher's context calculation and binds the challenge to the configuration, journal, allocator epoch and boot identity. It validates the record; it does not consume the challenge or prove freshness.

The current measurement path now derives results from complete raw observations without accepting caller-supplied passing flags. Its evidence envelope checks the expected profile and configuration digests, process-attempt facts and ordered file measurements. Actual supplied file bytes are rehashed before being passed into the complete configuration and measurement review.

Concrete launcher, evaluator and Python checks enforce their fixed paths, modes, startup arguments and capability settings. Each authority file must match its exact measurement role, preventing another record at the same path from standing in for it. The interpreter's loading requirements are checked against its supplied executable bytes.

A complete positive fixture now carries one native launcher identity through all those records and derives a current transcript from a different synthetic process than the historical accepted transcript. Additional tests reject altered interpreter measurement roles and capabilities even after their identities are recalculated. The combined focused and archive suite passes 111 tests. An earlier fixture-construction failure was corrected without weakening the validator.

blocks.label: Validation is connected; real startup is still ahead
blocks.text: This milestone runs Python validation with synthetic executable bytes and supplied process and descriptor facts. It does not execute the native launcher, establish real protected-handle custody, consume a challenge, publish a durable receipt or complete a coding task. The historical full-suite and packaged-snapshot results retain their original scope. Next comes protected-handle verification, one-use journal consumption, receipt publication and parent verification, followed by actual startup and the controlled coding demonstration.

sections.title: Testing one-use permission and saved startup receipts

blocks.text: The successor input reader now checks a real sealed memory file before interpreting its evidence. Disposable child processes accepted the exact required input and rejected missing seals, wrong names or permissions, writable or incorrectly inherited handles, malformed contents and a wrong expected profile digest. These cases test the input reader; they do not establish the complete protected process boundary.

A separate directory experiment passed ten checks using actual retained directory handles. It accepted the intended journal and receipt directories and rejected swapped handles, incorrect object identities, wrong ownership, weakened permissions, removed directories and closed handles. The fixed handoff reader checks process conditions and the inherited handle set before accessing measurement files. Its ordering tests do not simulate a successful full startup.

The evaluator now derives the startup receipt, invocation and consumption request from the complete successor review, then connects them to one-use consumption and durable publication. It writes the receipt without replacing an existing result, synchronizes the files and directory, and reopens the exact bytes it reviewed. A completion record alone cannot authorize the next stage; the native parent still has to verify the saved state independently.

Three isolated real-file cases passed under the launcher's user and group with no supplementary groups. Success saved the exact receipt and rejected reuse. Missing allocation produced no consume record or receipt. An existing receipt blocked publication, preserved the prior bytes and left the permission consumed, so another attempt could not turn that failure into success. File ownership and permissions were checked, and all temporary directories were removed.

The first durable experiment reached success and replay rejection but stopped at a test readback that omitted a required argument. That failed result was retained. Correcting the fixture produced the three passing cases without changing the workflow's validation rules. The related runtime, evaluator, source and archive suite passed 120 tests.

blocks.label: Next: the complete protected startup
blocks.text: These experiments use synthetic runtime measurements with real handles and files. They do not prove full native startup, independent parent acceptance, every crash point, power-loss recovery or a real coding task. The next work supplies independently trusted runtime inputs, packages the exact Python dependency set, connects the fixed evaluator entry point and verifies the parent handoff. Then the complete coding demonstration must cover success, failure, restart and cancellation before a fresh experimental release.

sections.title: Packaging the evaluator and testing its protected child process

blocks.text: The successor evaluator needs six project modules plus the package initializer. Isolated Python does not search the normal project directory, so a single-file replacement would not be a working installation. A staging tool now records the exact project bytes and tests them with site packages and the ordinary user environment excluded. A complete synthetic semantic fixture produces the same receipt as the checkout without importing test code into the child.

The import observation identifies 53 filesystem modules and nine mapped native files. Read-only inspection of those native files finds fourteen interpreter and library references, all matched within the observed set, including two imported Python extensions. Missing transitive dependencies and ambiguous library names are rejected. This establishes the observed dependency references; it does not prove every future dynamic import or deployment-specific loader search.

A disposable filesystem then placed the measured interpreter, standard library, project package and native dependencies at the intended startup paths. The first attempt stopped before Python started because the copied dynamic loader lacked execute permission. After that packaging error was corrected, a separate attempt passed with the required arguments, minimal environment, user and group, and no supplementary groups. All 53 filesystem imports matched their measured bytes and the exact expected receipt was produced. The 63 installed files stayed unchanged and cleanup removed the test filesystem.

A further fixture connected the actual protected child-process checks to the durable workflow. It used a private mount namespace, null standard streams, sealed read-only evidence, the two retained journal and receipt directories, and no extra inherited handles. All capability sets were empty, including the bounding set, and privilege gains were disabled. The child saved the receipt and rejected replay; the parent fixture independently reopened the consume and receipt files and confirmed their exact expected bytes.

A separate negative case deliberately retained the capability bounding set. The child was rejected before consuming permission or publishing a receipt. The initial allocation and the fixture's diagnostic report were the only files left in its mutable directories. Every fixture directory was subsequently removed; these experiments did not install the production runtime or change system Python.

The source now also connects the fixed-handle reader directly to the complete successor validation and durable workflow. This adapter accepts no caller-supplied runtime bytes, replacement evidence or alternate journal handles. Five composition tests cover its successful semantic path with mocked handoff and durable operations, changed file bytes, an independent configuration-pin mismatch, early handoff failure and forbidden input overrides. The combined focused runtime, evaluator, source, dependency and archive suite passes 129 tests.

blocks.label: The remaining native-launcher connection
blocks.text: The process fixtures still supply synthetic runtime measurements and trusted expectations through fixture data. They do not establish native-parent origin, independently accepted runtime deployment or the native parent's journal transaction. The newer fixed-handle adapter is covered by composition tests and is not part of the earlier staged package's recorded hashes. Next work must supply protected trust inputs, join real runtime-file rereads to the actual launcher, and complete startup before demonstrating coding success, failure, restart and cancellation. The historical full-suite and source-v10 results retain their original scope.

sections.title: Checking real runtime files and the native supervisor's journal

blocks.text: The connected evaluator now reads its sealed input and reopens the installed runtime files itself. Earlier tests supplied those file contents as fixture data. A disposable installation now binds the actual Python interpreter, package, standard-library and native-library bytes to the test deployment, then measures the installed files before handing control to the evaluator. The successful case completes validation, saves the consume record and receipt, and rejects replay. A separate case changes a configuration file after measurement while preserving its size and permissions; the evaluator detects the changed bytes and stops before saving either record.

Packaging exposed an empty Python package initializer that the existing nonempty-file rule would reject. The candidate installation uses deterministic compiled bytecode for that initializer, with isolated import and repeatability checks. A strengthened installation also measures the standard-library file used to locate Python's library directory. These are tested packaging choices; they do not establish an accepted production deployment.

Connecting the Python records to the native supervisor exposed another incompatibility: required multiline observations use escaped text in JSON, but the native text reader rejected every escape. A proposed repair adds a bounded decoder specifically for observation text. The native compatibility fixture passes six positive and twelve negative record checks plus thirteen decoder cases. Failed diagnostic attempts and a test-source compilation mistake are retained in the evidence. The complete proposed launcher builds and passes static executable review, but this new binary has not completed full startup or reproducibility qualification.

The next fixture invokes the actual native parent verification function with real credentials, a locked journal and a durable reservation. Valid records produce one committed transaction, clear the reservation and reject a second verification call. Reopening the journal preserves its exact committed control state. A malformed consume request produces no committed transaction. Recovery then permanently retires that pending reservation so it cannot be reused. Independent checks join the saved transaction, record identities, file hashes and receipt lengths. The temporary test filesystems are removed.

The refreshed focused suite passes 131 tests across successor runtime and evaluator validation, source-policy checks, Python packaging dependencies and source export. This is a current integration check, separate from the older source-v10 packaged validation totals and the individually recorded native execution experiments.

blocks.label: What this proves—and what remains
blocks.text: The native journal and parent verification path now have real execution evidence under controlled fixture conditions. Upstream deployment identities, accepted platform observations and some launcher state are still supplied by tests. The complete original launcher has not run a real coding task. The next integration must obtain expected inputs independently from protected deployment context, establish the actual startup measurements and connect that full path to the coding workflow.

sections.title: Testing the evaluator with a privileged supervisor

blocks.text: The evaluator now checks the real Linux parent process before and after reading its runtime files. It compares the sealed input's process ID, start time and boot identity with kernel observations, and requires the parent's exact credential and capability settings. Disposable process tests reject false process or boot claims even when the submitted evidence has been rehashed to be internally consistent. These observations establish process facts; they do not by themselves authenticate the parent's executable or the accepted deployment.

A fresh eight-file Python project package includes the new checks and passes isolated import and synthetic semantic validation. Its observed native dependencies remain nine files joined by fourteen references. The handoff changes passed a focused 138-test suite, separate from the historical packaged-source validation and the individually recorded execution experiments.

The combined executable test now uses a disposable privileged Python supervisor with the launcher's required credentials. It launches one evaluator at the intended interpreter and script paths, with the fixed arguments, environment, sealed input and retained journal directories. The evaluator drops all capabilities, verifies its actual parent, reopens the installed runtime files, completes semantic checks and saves its consume record and receipt. Replay is rejected, and the outer test harness reopens both saved files and confirms their exact bytes.

Two additional runs exercise failure through that same executable path. One changes the claimed parent process and rehashes the evidence; the other changes an installed file after measurement while preserving its metadata. Both stop before writing a consume record or receipt. All three runs remove their temporary filesystems and reap the supervised processes.

In parallel, a candidate reader for the fixed source configuration accepts no caller-selected paths or hashes. Seven real filesystem cases cover a valid root-owned read-only installation and rejection of changed bytes, symlinks, incorrect ownership or permissions, and a writable mount. That reader is tested separately and is not yet used by the combined executable fixture.

blocks.label: Remaining integration
blocks.text: The supervisor is test code, and accepted platform records plus some service, journal and attempt expectations still come from fixtures. The original native launcher has not completed this whole startup path. The remaining work must connect protected deployment and current journal context, the measured evaluator entry point and native parent verification, then demonstrate a real coding task through success, failure, interruption and cancellation.

sections.title: Replacing synthetic platform records with native measurements

blocks.text: The fixed source reader is now connected to the supervised executable fixture. The evaluator reads thirteen protected source and provider files from a root-owned read-only installation instead of accepting their contents from fixture input. The successful run saves the exact consume record and receipt and rejects replay. A separate run changes source bytes after measurement and is rejected before either record is written. The related focused suite passed 140 tests; these results remain separate from the older packaged-source totals.

Work then moved to executing the actual native platform-profile routine in a disposable delegated service. Its process credentials, namespace setup and kernel operations are real, while deployment identities and some initialization remain synthetic. This is a diagnostic step toward complete startup, not an accepted runtime or a completed coding job.

The native experiments found a concrete path-handling bug: several process-directory reads forbade symbolic links while using Linux's symbolic link for the current process. Proposed corrections use the actual numeric process ID and retain strict path checks. The baseline and snapshot reads additionally verify the process filesystem and use fixed relative filenames. These corrections advance the probe past setup, resource-group creation and initial child-process handle checks.

At that diagnostic milestone, the failure narrowed: the main profile child returns no measurement report, and the kernel reports that it was killed with SIGKILL. Recorded test-service counters show no out-of-memory kill, process-limit hit or CPU throttling. Simpler feature probes report success for child creation, process handles, namespaces, resource-group controls and filtering. Two communication probes report mismatches. These observations guide the investigation; they do not establish the cause of the kill or qualify the full profile.

Those initial native attempts failed the complete profile. The transient test services and temporary filesystems were removed, and failed attempts were retained alongside proposed fixes. The subsequent corrections and successful routine execution are described below.

blocks.label: What that milestone left open
blocks.text: The immediate work was to diagnose the child's termination and communication mismatches and verify complete native measurements. Those investigations have now advanced to the successful routine execution below. Independently trusted deployment, full startup and the real coding demonstration remain open.

sections.title: Native platform checks complete; full launcher builds

blocks.text: The corrected native platform-profile routine now completes in a disposable delegated service without diagnostic instrumentation. All twelve feature checks report completion, all 147 verification entries are populated, and internal cleanup succeeds. Independent checks confirm that the transient service's resource group and temporary filesystem are gone. Kernel operations are real, but deployment identities and some initial state remain synthetic; this is not full original-launcher startup.

Control experiments traced the earlier child termination to reusing a resource group after its mandatory kill test. The candidate keeps that test, proves the old group empty and removed, and creates a fresh group for the main child. Further corrections address process-directory lookup, empty optional mount fields and the prescribed handle used to reopen a private temporary filesystem.

Actual Linux message tests also exposed differences from the proposed packet rules. An explicit policy amendment preserves message lengths, ordering, truncation checks, attached-data checks and end-of-stream handling while correcting expected flags. The child report now carries the complete verification vector and reserves parent-only observations for the parent. Native checks cover 36 decoder cases, seven encoder rejection cases and an exact round trip.

A semantic audit found that the previous namespace observer measured process symbolic links rather than the namespace objects themselves. A normal parent and child can share a namespace while having different link identities. The corrected observer opens and checks the actual namespace objects, with a regression covering shared namespaces. Earlier successful executions therefore remain recorded but are not used as valid namespace-isolation evidence. Fifteen native parser cases also cover valid mount records and malformed or disallowed records.

These cumulative fixes are now consolidated into one proposed source set. A fresh complete native launcher build passed all five compile, assembly and link stages with warnings treated as errors and no diagnostics. Read-only executable checks passed for static structure, required symbols and memory permissions. The resulting launcher has not been executed; a successful build does not establish accepted deployment or startup.

blocks.label: Next integration steps
blocks.text: Review and version the changed policy and source bindings, update the evaluator's protected source checks, establish independently reviewed runtime and deployment inputs, and run the original launcher through full startup. Then complete one isolated coding task through success, failure, restart and cancellation before packaging the experimental GitHub release. The engine source has not yet been released publicly.

sections.title: Joining revised rules to the protected evaluator

blocks.text: The packet-rule correction now has a distinct profile identity. Historical rules remain intact, and the revised validator accepts only the defined changes. The native launcher embeds the new profile bindings; the Python evaluator reads the matching source set from fixed protected files. Downstream checks select the rules once from the trusted profile pin and do not retry another version after failure.

The proposed build contract now names the exact compiled launcher source and explicit linker script while retaining the historical source reference. Actual input bytes are checked separately from those declarations. The full native build and static executable checks pass. An unprivileged native test exercises the complete build-contract check against a synthetic deployment and rejects rehashed changes to the launcher pin, linker pin and linker options.

That native test initially rejected its nominally valid case because the synthetic deployment still contained older provider hashes. The failed attempt was preserved. Investigation found that Python checked deployment files and the source contract separately without directly joining the six provider roles. A regression reproduced the gap for every role. Python now requires each deployed provider's length and digest to match the pinned contract, and the fixtures use consistent source records. All 149 focused checks passed at that point; 23 targeted checks passed after the final source-pin migration.

A fresh package contains twelve project modules. Isolated execution observes 58 filesystem modules and nine native files, with fourteen declared native dependency references resolved. The package's synthetic semantic result matches the checkout. Seven real filesystem cases verify the protected source reader, including rejection of changed bytes, symbolic links, wrong permissions or ownership, and a writable mount.

The refreshed evaluator also runs at its intended paths under the disposable privileged Python supervisor, with sealed input, fixed handles, the expected identity and no child capabilities. It reopens protected source and runtime files, saves its consume record and receipt, and rejects replay. The parent independently reopens and verifies both outputs. A separate source-tampering case stops before either output is written. Temporary installations are removed. One mistyped output path stopped an earlier negative invocation before setup; a fresh attempt completed the negative test.

blocks.label: The boundary still to cross
blocks.text: These process tests still use synthetic acceptance records and a Python test supervisor. They do not establish independently accepted runtime deployment or full original native-launcher startup. The next work must provision and verify that real deployment, bind current platform measurements and runtime acceptance, and complete startup before demonstrating coding success, failure, restart and cancellation. No engine GitHub release has been published.

sections.title: Reproducible builds and the startup trust boundary

blocks.text: Two separate builds of the joined native source now produce identical bytes for all five assembly, object and executable outputs. The comparison checks actual files against recorded hashes, matching build inputs and settings, and the executable's static structure. This establishes repeatability for those two builds on this host; it does not establish cross-machine reproducibility or a working runtime.

The new parent-process guard retains a Linux process handle and process-directory handle until evaluation is finished with them. It can recheck parent identity, start time, credentials and liveness. Eight focused checks cover handle lifetime, cleanup after failure, changed identity or credentials, and a real parent-process exit. The exit test confirms that a child rejects its retained context after its parent dies.

A separate disposable experiment uses the intended parent and child identities and capability settings without mocking credential checks. The guard succeeds. Linux denies the unprivileged child access to the privileged parent's executable, which exposes a concrete integration constraint. Parent dumpability remains disabled and the child receives no extra privileges.

The next step is to bind protected deployment and service context to the parent identity observed by the kernel. Existing service-policy records describe intended settings, and the launcher creates its own live custody record; neither alone supplies independent executable authentication to the child. The new guard still needs integration with the evaluator's strict file-handle checks and durable result publication.

blocks.label: Still before complete startup
blocks.text: The privilege experiment uses a disposable Python parent, not the original native launcher. The guard is development code and is not yet in the staged evaluator package. Full startup, actual coding execution, failure and restart recovery, cancellation and an experimental engine release remain open.

sections.title: Native handoff tested; revised evaluator runs

blocks.text: The proposed startup admission components now include a protected process-bound record reader, durable publication that refuses existing records, a retained executable check and the transition from the privileged startup process to the launcher account. Focused tests cover stale records, unsafe filesystem permissions, concurrent publication, partial writes and sync failures. These components are not yet a complete installed startup service.

A native diagnostic verifies the privilege transition across execution of a retained file handle. The exact file capabilities pass the native credential checks; a copy without those capabilities is rejected. The listener-handoff experiment initially failed because it opened the executable before changing mount namespaces. A separate diagnostic observed that capabilities were not restored in that setup. Opening and measuring the executable after namespace setup corrected the experiment, and the executable guard now rejects a later namespace change.

The corrected native handoff accepts three null standard handles and two real listeners. It rejects an extra inherited handle and a listener assigned to the wrong role. These tests use private temporary filesystems, a diagnostic native entry point and synthetic role assignments. They establish the handoff behavior, not service-manager provenance or the complete original startup.

Reviewing the remaining startup code exposed three more process-file reads that forbade symbolic links while using Linux's current-process symbolic link. The actual kernel reproduced the failures. A proposed correction reads the fixed files relative to an existing verified process-directory handle. Native regression tests pass all three allowed reads, reject eight other paths, reproduce the old failures and confirm handle cleanup.

The correction passes the full native build and updated contract checks. Its new provider and build identities now match the protected Python reader and a freshly staged package. The executable guard also matches the new binary. Forty-nine focused checks passed at that point, separate from older full-suite and packaged-source totals.

Fresh supervised evaluator runs complete the updated protected-file reads, save and independently verify the durable result, and reject replay. A separate altered-source run stops before durable output. Both remove their temporary installations. The public progress claim remains limited: the supervisor is test code, upstream acceptance is synthetic, and the admission components are not yet joined to original native startup.

blocks.label: Next integration
blocks.text: Finish protected runtime configuration and service-manager context, join startup admission publication to the tested native handoff, and connect authenticated expectations to the evaluator. Then demonstrate a real isolated coding task through success, failure, restart and cancellation before preparing the experimental engine release.

sections.title: Protected startup components now run together

blocks.text: The new service-context reader has been exercised in an actual temporary service launched by Linux's service manager. It checks process identity, membership in the fixed service, namespace relationships and the manager's invocation record. It rejects use after a fork or a namespace change. A restricted-permission comparison showed that inspecting the manager needs one additional startup capability; the existing transition removes it before native execution.

A fixed configuration reader supplies the expected runtime, bundle and deployment identities from a protected read-only file. Six syntax tests and eleven real filesystem cases pass, including missing files, symlinks, wrong ownership or permissions, extra links, writable mounts and modification through a previously opened writable reference. The test identities are synthetic: file protection does not prove that a configuration has been reviewed or accepted.

The proposed root entry now connects service verification, configuration and executable checks, durable process-bound admission publication, privilege removal and execution of the measured file. Five composed cases pass. The valid case reaches native diagnostic success. An extra handle and malformed configuration stop before publication; a duplicate admission record remains unchanged; a listener assigned to the wrong role is rejected by the native diagnostic after publication.

The saved admission records match the observed process and the invocation independently reported by the service manager. Temporary services and files are removed, and the outer mount namespace is unchanged. Fifty-three focused component tests also pass. The composition uses a diagnostic executable, synthetic configuration and test-created listeners, so it does not demonstrate the full original launcher or a real coding job.

A subsequent compatibility review found an architectural conflict: the preserved native design explicitly excludes privileged Python, a pre-execution attester and the extra inspection capability used by the experimental wrapper. The passing diagnostic does not resolve that conflict or accept the wrapper for deployment. The project must resolve the architecture and service-policy change, or use an authentication approach compatible with direct native startup.

Independent of that design issue, the integrated evaluator now retains its parent-process handles through runtime reads and durable output. It rechecks identity and liveness at each use boundary and permits only its own additional handles. Seventy-seven focused checks pass, including parent-loss ordering and real descriptor checks. A fresh protected run saves and independently verifies its result and rejects replay; a false-parent run stops before durable writes. The initial negative-test attempt used an outdated expected error message and is preserved as a failed harness check.

blocks.label: Next integration
blocks.text: Resolve the startup wrapper's architecture compatibility before selecting a deployment design. Then connect executable and service authentication to the retained evaluator checks, review and provision the real runtime and service activation, run original startup, and demonstrate coding-task success, failure, restart and cancellation.

sections.title: Real evaluator entry now runs

blocks.text: Review of the original design showed that the native launcher already owns the startup decision. It verifies its inputs before creating the evaluator, then compares saved output against its own retained challenge, observations and journal state. A successful child exit is never enough. Development is continuing with that direct native startup model; the experimental privileged Python wrapper is not selected for deployment.

The new evaluator entry takes no arguments beyond the fixed launch contract. It reads sealed evidence and protected source files, reopens the runtime files, retains parent-process checks, performs the existing semantic validation, consumes the challenge once and publishes the receipt. The separate review APIs still reject mismatched independently supplied expectations. Shared internal routines preserve the validation and publication checks.

All 77 existing focused checks and nine new checks pass. The exact entry script also ran in a fresh isolated filesystem with no test-input file and no test diagnostic writer. The supervising fixture independently reopened both durable outputs and compared them with the expected bytes. Separate false-parent and protected-source-mutation cases exited without publishing a consume record or receipt. Temporary installations were removed.

These executions still use a disposable privileged Python supervisor and synthetic upstream acceptance. They establish that the real evaluator entry works under that handoff, not that the full native launcher has started or that a runtime deployment is accepted. The child checks kernel parent facts but does not independently attest the parent's executable; the native launcher retains responsibility for authenticating its inputs and verifying the final durable result.

blocks.label: Next integration
blocks.text: Bind the real entry and its staged dependencies into the actual deployment, establish the required platform acceptance and protected service and journal state, then run the original native startup path from its first checks through final verification. After that, demonstrate an isolated coding task through success, failure, restart and cancellation before preparing the experimental engine release.

sections.title: Candidate syscall filter tested

blocks.text: Separating actual runtime file collection from synthetic test fixtures exposed three missing deployment roles: the filter compiler, verifier and compiled filter. Those now have real artifacts. The compiler follows the exact pinned syscall policy and repository table, permits the 100 known calls outside the deny set, and rejects other native numbers. It uses no host-header lookup or weaker fallback.

The verifier checks the filter's decisions independently of the compiler's instruction ordering. Its restricted instruction format lets it exhaust the possible decision classes, including unknown numbers. Tests show that equivalent reorderings pass while weakened architecture checks, forbidden or unknown allowances, missing required allowances, invalid jumps and changed source pins fail. The compiler and verifier share the pinned policy reader.

Ten filter tests and seven file-collection tests pass. Two disposable unprivileged children also installed the exact compiled filter. The expected allowed call succeeded; a forbidden local socket call, a number absent from the pinned table and a future number returned permission errors. An x32 request terminated as required. Both children were reaped. The foreign-architecture rule was checked in the filter structure; these tests did not switch the running kernel-call architecture.

A subsequent minimal interpreter probe exposed a practical incompatibility. The pinned Python interpreter failed during startup with a TLS allocation error after the filter was installed; the same interpreter completed successfully in an unfiltered comparison. Both children were reaped. The unfiltered run served only as a diagnostic comparison. Several startup-related calls are absent from the pinned table, and at that stage the exact denied call had not been isolated. The follow-up below records the diagnosis and proposed fix.

The updated inventory contains 93 actual files and no missing required launcher role names. File presence is not deployment acceptance: dependency ordering, loader aliases, complete identities, platform qualification and protected service and journal setup still need to be joined. These tests do not demonstrate original native startup or a real coding job.

blocks.label: Integration work identified
blocks.text: The failure identified runtime coverage of the pinned syscall table as the next issue to resolve. Complete deployment, platform acceptance, original native startup and coding-task success, failure, restart and cancellation remain required before an experimental engine release.

sections.title: Python starts under the proposed filter

blocks.text: A read-only diagnostic traced a disposable process and found an architecture setup call denied immediately before the earlier TLS startup error. A separate successful baseline used eight calls missing from the pinned table. An explicit proposal adds those eight definitions; it preserves the exact deny list and rejects unknown numbers.

The proposed filter was compiled and checked against its own exact table pin. The interpreter then completed a minimal program with the filter enforced, without tracing or an unfiltered fallback. Separate disposable kernel checks confirmed that socket creation and unknown calls remain denied, and x32 calls terminate the process. All test children were reaped. Twenty-one focused tests passed, including rejection of mismatched table versions and weakened guards.

The proposed table has also been joined to a new native source and build record. All five isolated build stages completed successfully. The native executable is byte-for-byte identical to the preceding build; the separate candidate filter carries the changed syscall allowances. This is build evidence, not runtime acceptance.

The source version has since been carried through the protected reader and a fresh Python staging. Native helper execution passed eight source-pin cases and five build-contract cases, including rejection of the preceding table against the revised deployment record. Seven protected-file custody cases passed. The freshly staged evaluator produced the expected durable output in a supervised disposable environment; false-parent and altered-source cases were rejected before output. The first invocation lacked required test-harness options and was rejected before setup; a separate corrected attempt passed.

The actual file inventory now combines that tested evaluator, protected source records, rebuilt native executable and verified filter. It contains 93 files with no missing required launcher role names. File presence is still not deployment acceptance: the supervised tests use synthetic acceptance records and a disposable Python parent, so they do not exercise the complete native launcher.

The deployment layout now has a concrete proposal too. A fresh supervised evaluator run succeeded using three explicit file aliases and no directory shortcut. The actual file collector then produced 89 ordered runtime objects and seven configuration artifacts, covering 93 regular files. Existing validators rederived the record identities and checked the raw bytes. Six focused tests passed, including changed-byte rejection, object ordering, alias constraints and collection without importing test fixtures. This is one proposed launcher record, not an accepted complete runtime.

blocks.label: Scope and next step
blocks.text: Next, complete the other required deployment roles and review the configuration policies. Establish actual installed custody, platform acceptance, protected stores, service and socket setup, and runtime activation. Then exercise original native startup and the real coding-task success, failure, restart and cancellation paths before preparing an experimental release.

sections.title: What still needs to connect

blocks.alt: Three stages of progress: the verified source-v9 snapshot has a repeatable source export and offline checks; current development tests cancellation and integration with focused checks; the next demonstration must complete one isolated coding task through success, failure, restart and cancellation. Production qualification remains open.
blocks.caption: Figure 2. The earlier source-v9 milestone and the intended integration stages. The verified package has since advanced to source-v10; the complete workflow demonstration remains pending.

blocks.text: The remaining work connects authenticated task delivery, a protected execution identity and the final runtime environment. Stopping a task must also stop the work it started, with evidence covering child processes, interrupted callers and the Windows-to-Linux boundary.

The proposed policy changes still need acceptance, and the actual runtime still needs qualification: checks that the intended executable, libraries, permissions and launch conditions are enforced together. Passing component tests does not establish those properties for a live coding task.
The evolutionary part also has a clear limit today. The current convergence process uses a population of one. Broader search across multiple competing candidates remains future work.

sections.title: The next demonstration

items.title: Connect the existing authority chain
body: Reconcile the saved review dispatch with the successor runtime-policy model, then join accepted deployment and runtime custody to the tested V2 delivery path, per-step claims and protected launcher. Demonstrate that lost responses and restarts cannot trigger another execution.

items.title: Extend stopping and recovery evidence
body: Build on the demonstrated cleanup and cancellation paths. Resolve escaped-descendant containment and verify service restart recovery and concurrent request handling through the complete workflow, with bounded behavior and durable results.

items.title: Complete one real coding task
body: Use an isolated copy of a small test project. Capture a proposed patch and its test results while preserving the original. Demonstrate success, a deliberate test failure, replay or restart handling, and cancellation.

items.title: Build a fresh experimental release
body: Rebuild from the updated source, repeat installation in a clean environment and validate the new export. Publish reproducible instructions with a precise account of the demonstrated capabilities and remaining limits.

sections.title: How progress will be reported

blocks.text: Each update will identify the artifact or source state behind its results, describe failures as well as successes, and separate implemented behavior from planned capabilities. Progress toward a complete coding workflow will be measured by demonstrated behavior, including recovery and stopping. Public updates summarize the findings without exposing private logs, local paths or internal authority records.
